data.body:
Crew slot: 40 minutes. HOWL: Responsibility. "I take responsibility for my success as a learner."

This week you build one small system so that arriving prepared and finishing on time stops depending on willpower.

1. Read **One System for the Week** (10 minutes).
2. Learn the **Glossary** words, then win the **Matching** game.
3. Keep the **Three Parts of a System** chart open.
4. Sort the cards in **System or Willpower?**
5. Take the quiz. Question 2 is about why willpower fails.
6. Open the SEL Hub and choose [Executive Function](#sel-hub/execfunction?station=sel_station_crew_launch_system). Build your capture spot and launch check there. Then open [Goal Setter](#sel-hub/goals?station=sel_station_crew_launch_system) and set one goal for the week that your system will carry.
7. Use the **Sentence Frames** to write your system in three lines.
8. Lock it in with **Remember Capture, Launch, Reset**.
9. Finish with the **Design Challenge: My One System**, and test it for a week.

Your commitment: this week, do the launch check at the end of every day, and count how many mornings you had everything. 🎒

Clicking a tool link above also starts your Crew station for this week, so the time you spend in the tools and the self-check stay together in one place. It stays active until you exit it, so come back later in the week to mark the self-check. You can find it again under SEL Stations in the History panel. 📌

history.title: One System for the Week
history.data:
## One System for the Week

**HOWL: "I take responsibility for my success as a learner."**

Two of the Responsibility behaviors in the King **HOWLs** are about the boring, powerful stuff: arrive **prepared** for class, and complete assignments **thoughtfully** and on time. Nobody gets a standing ovation for having a charged laptop. But almost every bad week starts with a small thing that was not where it needed to be.

Here is the trap. Most people try to fix a messy week with **willpower**. "I will just remember." "I will try harder." Willpower is real, but it runs out, and it runs out fastest on the days you need it most. A **system** does not run out. A system is a small set of steps you do the same way every time, so that your brain does not have to decide anything.

A good system for middle school has three parts. A **capture** spot: one place where every assignment and due date goes the moment you hear it. Not your memory. Not three places. One. A **launch** check: one look at tomorrow before you leave school, so that whatever you need is in the bag tonight, not in your locker at 8:04. And a weekly **reset**: ten minutes once a week to look at the whole week ahead, notice the big things, and split them into pieces.

Here is a fictional **Crew** example. Marcus is smart and disorganized. He writes assignments on his hand, on sticky notes, and sometimes nowhere. He arrives without his science notebook about twice a week. His Crew leader, Mr. Bell, does not tell him to try harder. He asks Marcus to pick one capture spot. Marcus picks the notes app on his laptop, because it is always open. For two weeks, every assignment goes there, and nowhere else. Then Mr. Bell asks him to add a launch check: last two minutes of the day, open the notes, look at tomorrow, pack the bag. By the third week, Marcus has his notebook every day. Nothing about his brain changed. His system did.

Completing work thoughtfully is the other half. Thoughtfully does not mean slowly. It means the work got the kind of attention it needed. A system helps here too, because when you split a big assignment into pieces during the weekly reset, you stop doing all of it at 11 p.m. on the night before. Work done at 11 p.m. is rarely thoughtful.

One more thing. A system is yours. The capture spot can be paper or a screen. The launch check can be a list or a photo of your locker. The weekly reset can be Sunday night or Monday during Crew. What matters is that it is one system, you use it the same way each time, and you fix it when it breaks instead of going back to willpower.

This week you build one. Not the perfect one. One you will actually use on Thursday.

data.def: A small set of steps you do the same way every time, so your brain does not have to decide.
Deciding to try harder in the moment. Real, but it runs out.
Writing something down the moment you hear it, in one place.
A one-minute look at tomorrow before you leave school today.
A ten-minute weekly look at the whole week ahead.
Having what you need, where you need it, when class starts.
Work that got the kind of attention it needed, not just work that got done.
A piece of a big assignment small enough to finish in one sitting.
Something you do without deciding to, because you have done it the same way many times.
A small group of students and one adult who meet regularly to support each other and reflect on learning. EL Education's word for advisory.
Habit of Work and Learning: a way of working that your school teaches and scores separately from academic grades. At King, the three are Respect, Responsibility, and Perseverance.

questions.question: What does the reading say a system is?
options: A planner your school gives you at the start of the year
A small set of steps you do the same way every time
A promise to yourself to try harder when things get busy
An app that reminds you when things are due
questions.correctAnswer: A small set of steps you do the same way every time

questions.question: Why does the reading say willpower is not enough?
options: Because willpower is not real for most students in middle school
Because teachers do not give credit for effort alone
Because it runs out, and fastest on the days you need it most
Because using willpower means you did not plan ahead
questions.correctAnswer: Because it runs out, and fastest on the days you need it most

questions.question: What changed for Marcus by the third week?
options: His brain changed, and he became a more organized person
Mr. Bell started packing his bag with him each day
He switched to a paper planner that worked better
Nothing about his brain changed; his system did
questions.correctAnswer: Nothing about his brain changed; his system did

questions.question: What does "thoughtfully" mean in "complete assignments thoughtfully"?
options: The work got the kind of attention it needed
The work was done slowly and carefully every time
The work was checked by an adult before turning it in
The work was finished the day it was assigned
questions.correctAnswer: The work got the kind of attention it needed

questions.question: Your launch check keeps failing because you forget to do it. What does the reading say to do?
options: Go back to remembering, since the system did not work
Change nothing and hope that it works better next time
Fix the system by checking which part of it failed
Switch to a totally new system at the start of each week
questions.correctAnswer: Fix the system by checking which part of it failed

questions.question: Name the three parts of a system and the time span each one covers.
questions.expectedAnswer: Capture spot (the moment you hear it), launch check (end of each day), weekly reset (once a week).

| Criteria | 1 - Starting | 3 - Getting There | 5 - Crew Ready |
|---|---|---|---|
| One capture spot | Several places or memory | One place named | One place named, with when it gets used |
| Launch check | None | A time named | A time, what to look at, and what to pack |
| Fixable | No plan for breaking | Names the weak part | Names the weak part and the fix |

data.question: What is Crew, anyway?
data.answer: Crew is your school's word for a small group of students and one adult who meet regularly to check in, set goals, and work through hard things together. It comes from EL Education, the school model King has used since 1992, and from an old idea about ships: everyone on board is crew, not a passenger. Read more on [King's EL page](https://king.portlandschools.org/about/learning-models) or [EL Education's Crew page](https://www.eleducation.org/crew).

data.question: What is a HOWL?
data.answer: A Habit of Work and Learning. Your school scores three of them, apart from your academic grades: Respect ("I am a respectful member of the King community"), Responsibility ("I take responsibility for my success as a learner"), and Perseverance ("I persevere to produce high quality work"). Teachers score them; Crew is where you practice them. The statements are on [King's grading guide](https://king.portlandschools.org/families/handbook/handbook-interior/~board/king-student-family-handbook/post/grading-guide).

data.question: What if I like using several places?
data.answer: Several places means the assignment can be in the one you did not check. One capture spot is the whole point. You can copy it elsewhere later; it lands in one place first.

data.question: Paper or screen?
data.answer: Whichever one is always with you and always open. For some people that is the notes app. For some it is one small notebook. Pick, then stop switching.

data.question: What if the launch check takes too long?
data.answer: Then it is doing too much. It is one look at tomorrow and packing the bag. Two minutes. If it takes ten, you are doing the weekly reset by accident.

data.question: I built a system and it fell apart in a week. Did I fail?
data.answer: No. Systems break. Ask which part failed. Usually it is one part, and it usually needs to be smaller, not bigger.

data.question: How does this connect to my HOWL grade?
data.answer: The Responsibility HOWL includes arriving prepared and completing assignments thoughtfully and on time. A system is how those happen on the days you do not feel like it.

cards.aiExample: Catch it, Check it, Clear it. Catch the assignment when you hear it, check tomorrow before you leave, clear the week on Sunday. Three C-words in the order of the day, the evening, and the week.
cards.mapping: Catch is the capture spot, check is the launch check, clear is the weekly reset. The order runs from the smallest time span to the largest, which is the order you do them.

history.title: Design Challenge: My One System

data.title: My One System
data.instructions: Design a system with all three parts, run it for one school week, keep a simple morning count of "had everything" versus "missing something," and revise the part that broke.
data.fitReason: The HOWL behaviors are arriving prepared and completing assignments thoughtfully and on time. A designed, tested, and revised system is how those become reliable rather than a matter of effort on the day.

brief.context: You have read about capture, launch, and reset. Now you build your own version, for your bag, your locker, your classes, and your week.
brief.role: A student designing a system for themselves
brief.audience: You. Then your Crew, who will hear the one-week result and the one change you made.
brief.drivingQuestion: What is the smallest three-part system that gets me to every class prepared this week, and which part needs to change after I test it?
brief.seedDirection: Pick one capture spot you already have with you every day. Set the launch check to the same two minutes daily. Put the weekly reset on a day you can actually keep. Then run it and count mornings.
lockedLessonFacts: A system is a small set of steps you do the same way every time, so that your brain does not have to decide anything.
A good system has three parts: a capture spot, a launch check, and a weekly reset.
Willpower runs out; a system does not.
When a system breaks, fix the system instead of going back to willpower.
openQuestions: Which capture spot is truly always with me?
When are the two minutes for the launch check that I will not skip?
Which day can the weekly reset actually happen?
What is my biggest assignment in the next two weeks, and what are its chunks?
stakeholders: The teachers whose classes you arrive at
Anyone at home who helps you get out the door
criteria: All three parts are named with a specific time and place
The system was run for at least four school days
A morning count was kept (had everything or missing something)
One part was revised based on what broke, with the reason
Uses at least three glossary words correctly
constraints: The launch check is two minutes or less
The weekly reset is ten minutes or less
No new apps or supplies required
brief.deliverable: A system card (three lines: capture, launch, reset), the morning count for the week, and one sentence about what you changed and why.

parallelExample.context: A fictional student set her launch check for the walk to the bus.
parallelExample.move: By Wednesday she had skipped it twice because she was talking to friends. She moved it to the last two minutes of her final class, at her desk, and had everything the next three mornings. She did not change the capture spot or the reset; only the part that broke.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: It shows that a broken part is a location or timing problem, not a character problem, and that you change one part rather than the whole system.

supports.frameStarter: My capture spot is ____. My launch check is at ____. My reset is on ____.
frameChoices: This week I had everything ____ out of ____ mornings.
The part that broke was ____, because ____.
coachPrompts: If you had everything five out of five mornings, what made the system easy? Could it survive a bad week?
Which teacher would notice first if this system worked?

data.coachHint: Students often design a system that is too big. If the plan has more than three parts or needs new supplies, help them cut it. Small systems get used.
data.sourceExcerpt: A system is yours. The capture spot can be paper or a screen. The launch check can be a list or a photo of your locker. What matters is that it is one system, you use it the same way each time, and you fix it when it breaks instead of going back to willpower.
